newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Sweden's Investor to invest abroad.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Sweden's Investor to invest abroad.

text.p: Swedish industrial investment group Investor AB, which has core stakes in most of the country's top companies, said on Monday it planned to invest 10 percent of its funds abroad.

Managing director Claes Dahlback was asked at a news conference what Investor intended to do with the capital gain of 12.4 billion crowns ($1.87 billion) from selling its controlling stake in truck and bus-maker Scania AB in April.

"We envisage placing 10 percent of our investments in non-Swedish companies in sectors including information technology, health care and the financial sector," he said. "Our strategy will become clear once we make the first big investment."
The chief executive rebutted criticism arising from the Scania share's underperformance since Investor divested a 55 percent stake.
"Scania was sold at the right price," he said, adding that it was impossible to predict the costs of switching over to new models, and the adverse impact of the stronger Swedish crown.

Now a stand-alone company no longer consolidated in Investor, Scania reported on November 7 a sharp fall in nine-month profit after financial items of 2.14 billion crowns versus 3.51 billion a year earlier.
Its shares were trading at 167 crowns on Monday compared to a year high of 200 crowns.

Investor, the main investment vehicle of Sweden's industrial dynasty, the Wallenberg group, counts pharmaceuticals Astra, technology group Incentive and forestry concern Stora among its blue-chip portfolio.

Investor said the market value of those main holdings had risen to 53.12 billion crowns ($8 billion) at end-September from 49.28 billion at the end of 1995, but figures showed the increase would have been greater if Scania were excluded.

Investor said its net worth, considered the most appropriate figure on which to judge an investment company, rose to 73.2 billion crowns by September 30 compared with 51.23 billion at the end of last year.
This equated to 366 crowns per share compared with 257 crowns.
Net worth grew further to 74.11 billion crowns as of November 13 this year, Investor said in its nine-month report.
Saab AB, which embraces Saab's aerospace and defence companies but not Saab Automobile, is still wholly owned by Investor.
It reported a fall in profit after financial income and expenses to 84 million crowns from 223 million at the same time last year.
Saab Aircraft said income from manufacturing the Saab 340 and Saab 2000 planes continued to be negative.
Saab reported civilian aircraft sales worth 2.08 billion crowns ($314 million) in the nine months ended September 30 compared with 1.77 billion a year earlier but put no figure on the net loss.
"Competition from recently established jet programmes is very severe in the 50 passenger segment where Saab 2000 is sold," Saab said in a statement.
By September, Saab Military Aircraft had delivered 27 of 30 JAS 39 Gripen aircraft ordered by the Swedish Air Force.
The order backlog includes a further 110 planes, and on December 13 the Swedish parliament will decide whether to authorise further orders.
Saab group's new orders for the first nine months were 5.69 million crowns compared with 4.2 billion, and the order backlog at the end of September was 20.54 billion crowns against 21.29 billion.
Saab Automobile, jointly owned by Investor and America's General Motors Corp, did not report nine-month figures.
($1=6.62 crowns)
